source: High Country Fly Fishing Guides and Locals

conditions.overall: Valley rivers across WNC are low, clear, and warm due to a dry spring rolling into a dry summer, making fishing them hard a risk to released trout. High-elevation headwater streams and spring-fed feeder creeks are still running cold and holding willing fish.

tactics: Observe the 68-degree water-temperature rule — if valley water hits 68°F or above, move to high-elevation streams instead of fishing low, warm river water.
Go high: two thousand feet of elevation and a few ridgelines back puts you on small wild trout streams still running cold and mostly free of crowds.
Target headwater freestones, spring-fed feeder creeks, and brook trout blue-lines tucked into the highest folds of the Blue Ridge during drought summer conditions.
Approach high-country wild fish carefully — these fish are smaller, wilder, and less forgiving of a sloppy approach than hatchery-supported fish in valley runs.
Use terrestrial patterns as the foundation of a summer fly box on skinny mountain water at high elevation.

waters.name: Davidson River (lower)
waters.note: By 9 a.m. water temperature reached 71°F; fish were not moving or feeding even in runs that should produce. Low, clear, and warm — not recommended for hard fishing due to trout stress risk.

elevation_note: High Country streams (Boone, 3300-4000ft) run 1-2 weeks behind lower-elevation WNC
